title: Two simultaneous withdrawals leave the wrong balance
concept: Lost update: read-modify-write needs optimistic locking and a retry
symptom: Withdrawing 30 and 50 from a balance of 100 at the same time should leave 20. It leaves 70 or 50, as if one of the withdrawals never happened.
failingTest:
import unittest

from sched import run_all
from service import AccountService
from store import AccountStore


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_no_withdrawal_is_lost(self):
        store = AccountStore({"acc": 100})
        service = AccountService(store)
        amounts = [30, 50]
        results = run_all(*[service.withdraw("acc", cents) for cents in amounts])
        paid_out = sum(cents for cents, result in zip(amounts, results) if isinstance(result, int))
        balance, _ = store.read("acc")
        self.assertEqual(balance, 100 - paid_out)

import unittest

from sched import run_all
from service import AccountService, InsufficientFunds
from store import AccountStore


class Regression(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_both_withdrawals_succeed_when_there_is_enough_money(self):
        store = AccountStore({"acc": 100})
        service = AccountService(store)
        results = run_all(service.withdraw("acc", 30), service.withdraw("acc", 50))
        self.assertTrue(all(isinstance(r, int) for r in results), results)
        self.assertEqual(store.read("acc")[0], 20)

    def test_three_at_once_all_succeed(self):
        store = AccountStore({"acc": 100})
        service = AccountService(store)
        results = run_all(*[service.withdraw("acc", 10) for _ in range(3)])
        self.assertTrue(all(isinstance(r, int) for r in results), results)
        self.assertEqual(store.read("acc")[0], 70)

    def test_a_withdrawal_that_would_overdraw_is_rejected(self):
        store = AccountStore({"acc": 40})
        service = AccountService(store)
        results = run_all(service.withdraw("acc", 30), service.withdraw("acc", 30))
        self.assertEqual(sum(isinstance(r, int) for r in results), 1)
        self.assertEqual(sum(isinstance(r, InsufficientFunds) for r in results), 1)
        self.assertEqual(store.read("acc")[0], 10)

    def test_a_lone_withdrawal_just_works(self):
        store = AccountStore({"acc": 100})
        self.assertEqual(run_all(AccountService(store).withdraw("acc", 25)), [75])
rootCause: withdraw reads the balance, waits, then writes balance - cents back. Two withdrawals read the same 100 before either writes, so the second write overwrites the first: a lost update. The write must be conditional on the row's version, and a failed (stale) write must be retried from a fresh read.

wrongFixes.whyWrong: Checking the version stops the lost update, but with no retry the loser gets a Conflict error and no money, even though the account had enough for both withdrawals.

turns.text: Two withdrawals at the same time (30 and 50 from 100) leave the balance at 70 or 50 instead of 20. Fix it.
That is a lost update: both read 100 and write back their own result. I'll add optimistic locking, so a write only succeeds if the row has not changed since it was read.
test_failing: OK (1 test)
Fixed. The store now refuses a stale write, so the balance can never be wrong.

transcript.verdict: Right idea, half the job. The store now rejects the stale write, but nothing retries it, so one of the two customers gets a Conflict error and no money, even though there was plenty. The failing test only checks that the balance is consistent, not that both withdrawals went through; the regression suite does.

grading.question: Why does reading, waiting and writing back lose an update?
grading.ideal: Both transactions start from the same old value, so the later write silently overwrites the earlier one.

grading.question: How does a version column prevent it, and what must the caller then do?
grading.ideal: The write only applies if the version is unchanged; otherwise it fails and the caller re-reads and retries.

grading.question: Name two other ways to avoid a lost update.
grading.ideal: Lock the row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), or do the arithmetic in the database in one atomic statement.

title: An AI-written paginator hides the last page
concept: Reviewing an AI fix: ceiling division and its edge cases
symptom: An assistant wrote the pagination helper. Lists whose length is not a multiple of the page size report one page too few, so the last few items can never be reached through the API.
failingTest:

        response = list_response(ITEMS, page=3, per_page=10)
        self.assertEqual(response["items"], [20, 21, 22, 23, 24])
        self.assertEqual(response["total_pages"], 3)

title: Two transfers in opposite directions hang forever
concept: Deadlock: acquire locks in one global order
symptom: A transfer from Alice to Bob works. So does one from Bob to Alice. But when both happen at the same time, neither finishes and the test run ends with Deadlock.

files.bank.py:
from sched import yield_control


class InsufficientFunds(Exception):
    pass


class Bank:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active = 0  # transfers inside their critical section right now
        self.peak = 0    # the most that were ever inside at once

    async def transfer(self, source, target, cents):
        async with source.lock:
            await yield_control()  # e.g. a fraud check on the sending account
            async with target.lock:
                self.active += 1
                self.peak = max(self.peak, self.active)
                try:
                    await yield_control()
                    if source.balance < cents:
                        raise InsufficientFunds(source.id)
                    source.balance -= cents
                    target.balance += cents
                finally:
                    self.active -= 1

class InsufficientFunds(Exception):
    pass


class Bank:
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = Lock()
        self.active = 0  # transfers inside their critical section right now
        self.peak = 0    # the most that were ever inside at once

    async def transfer(self, source, target, cents):
        async with self._lock:
            async with source.lock:
                await yield_control()  # e.g. a fraud check on the sending account
                async with target.lock:
                    self.active += 1
                    self.peak = max(self.peak, self.active)
                    try:
                        await yield_control()
                        if source.balance < cents:
                            raise InsufficientFunds(source.id)
                        source.balance -= cents
                        target.balance += cents
                    finally:
                        self.active -= 1

        if self.inventory.available(sku) < quantity:

        await self.payments.charge(user, price_cents * quantity)
        self.inventory.reserve(sku, quantity)

symptom: The nightly export job overrides batch_size to 50. After that, the hourly job, which overrides nothing, also runs with batches of 50, and its retry attempts change too when nightly raises them.

import unittest

from job import ExportJob


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):

class EventTable:
    """An in-memory stand-in for the events table: id is unique, created_at is not."""

    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = [dict(r) for r in rows]
        self.queries = 0

    def page_after(self, created_after, limit):
        """SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?"""
        self.queries += 1
        hits = [r for r in self.rows if created_after is None or r["created_at"] > created_after]
        hits.sort(key=lambda r: r["created_at"])
        return hits[:limit]

class EventTable:

    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = [dict(r) for r in rows]
        self.queries = 0

    def page_after(self, after, limit):
        """SELECT * FROM events WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT ?

        after is the (created_at, id) of the last row already seen, or None for the first page. Ordering
        by a unique key makes the position of every row exact, even when timestamps are equal.
        """
        self.queries += 1
        key = lambda r: (r["created_at"], r["id"])
        hits = [r for r in self.rows if after is None or key(r) > after]
        hits.sort(key=key)
        return hits[:limit]

        self.queries = 0

        self.queries += 1
        hits = [r for r in self.rows if created_after is None or r["created_at"] >= created_after]

class EventTable:

    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = [dict(r) for r in rows]
        self.queries = 0

        """SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= ? ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?"""
        self.queries += 1
        hits = [r for r in self.rows if created_after is None or r["created_at"] >= created_after]

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    doc_id: str
    start: int  # where text[0] is in the original document
    text: str


def chunk_by_paragraph(doc_id, text):
    """One chunk per blank-line-separated paragraph, with surrounding whitespace trimmed."""
    chunks = []
    position = 0
    for raw in text.split("\n\n"):
        trimmed = raw.strip()
        if trimmed:

            chunks.append(Chunk(doc_id, position + leading, trimmed))
        position += len(raw) + 2
    return chunks

class FakeDB:
    """A stand-in for a SQL database that counts how much work it is asked to do."""

        self._authors = dict(authors)  # id -> row
        self.queries = 0
        self.rows_read = 0

        self.queries += 1
        self.rows_read += len(self._books)
        return [dict(book) for book in self._books]

    def select_author(self, author_id):
        """SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id = ?"""
        self.queries += 1
        row = self._authors.get(author_id)
        self.rows_read += 1 if row else 0
        return dict(row) if row else None

    def select_authors(self, author_ids):
        """SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id IN (...)"""
        self.queries += 1
        rows = [dict(self._authors[i]) for i in sorted(set(author_ids)) if i in self._authors]
        self.rows_read += len(rows)
        return rows

    def select_all_authors(self):

        self.queries += 1
        self.rows_read += len(self._authors)

title: tail runs out of memory on big logs
concept: Streaming with a bounded buffer
symptom: tail() returns the right lines, but on a 20 GB log the process is killed for memory. It only needs 10 lines.
failingTest:
import unittest

from fakefile import FakeFile


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):

        self.assertEqual(tail(f, 3), ["c\n", "d\n", "e\n"])
rootCause: readlines() materializes every line before slicing, so memory is O(file size). A bounded buffer of n lines (deque with maxlen) gives O(n) memory in one pass.

turns.text: tail() runs out of memory on a 20 GB log. It only needs the last few lines.

test_regression: OK (4 tests)

symptom: Users with unread messages are served from the cache, but users with zero unread cause a database query on every single page view, so most of your quiet accounts hammer the database.

import unittest

from clock import FakeClock
from profiles import FakeDB, ProfileService
from ttl_cache import TTLCache


class Regression(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.clock = FakeClock()
        self.db = FakeDB({"ada": 3, "bob": 7})
        self.service = ProfileService(TTLCache(self.clock, ttl=60), self.db)

    def test_a_count_is_cached(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("ada"), 3)
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("ada"), 3)
        self.assertEqual(self.db.calls, 1)

    def test_a_cached_count_is_reloaded_after_it_expires(self):
        self.service.unread_count("ada")
        self.clock.advance(60)
        self.db.unread["ada"] = 4
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("ada"), 4)
        self.assertEqual(self.db.calls, 2)

    def test_users_are_cached_separately(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("ada"), 3)
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("bob"), 7)
        self.assertEqual(self.db.calls, 2)

    def test_an_expired_zero_is_reloaded_too(self):
        self.db.unread["ada"] = 0
        self.service.unread_count("ada")
        self.clock.advance(61)
        self.db.unread["ada"] = 2
        self.assertEqual(self.service.unread_count("ada"), 2)
rootCause: get_or_load asks 'if value:', so a cached 0 (or '', [], False) looks exactly like a cache miss, and the loader runs again every time. The cache has to tell 'nothing stored' from 'a falsy value stored', with a sentinel or by testing the key, while still honouring expiry.

wrongFixes.whyWrong: Testing 'key in self._data' stops the reloads, but it skips the expiry check that get() performs, so an expired entry is served forever and never refreshed.

turns.text: Users with zero unread messages hit the database on every page view.
get_or_load checks 'if value:', so a cached 0 looks exactly like a miss. I check whether the key is stored instead of whether the value is truthy.
test_failing: OK (1 test)
Fixed: zero counts are served from the cache.

transcript.verdict: The membership test bypasses get(), and with it the expiry check, so an expired entry is served forever. The cache needs a miss signal that is not a falsy value, such as a sentinel object.

grading.question: Why is `if value:` the wrong test for a cache hit?
grading.ideal: It is false for 0, empty strings and empty collections, so valid cached results are treated as misses.

grading.question: What is a sentinel, and why use object() for it?
grading.ideal: A unique marker that no real value can equal, so 'missing' is distinguishable from every legitimate value including None.

grading.question: What other behaviour must a fix preserve?
grading.ideal: Expiry: entries must still be reloaded once their ttl has passed.

title: The router matches the wrong routes
concept: Pattern matching: segment boundaries, normalising input and route precedence
symptom: Three bugs from the API team: /users/1/posts is served by the single-user handler, /users/1/ returns 404 while /users/1 works, and /users/me hits the user-by-id handler with id='me' because that route was registered first.
failingTest:
import unittest
from router import Router


def make():
    r = Router()
    r.add("/users/<id>", "user")
    r.add("/users/me", "me")
    r.add("/users/<id>/posts", "posts")
    r.add("/", "home")
    return r


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_a_parameter_does_not_swallow_slashes(self):
        handler, params = make().match("/users/1/posts")
        self.assertEqual((handler, params), ("posts", {"id": "1"}))

    def test_a_trailing_slash_is_ignored(self):
        self.assertEqual(make().match("/users/1/"), ("user", {"id": "1"}))

    def test_a_fixed_route_beats_a_parameter_route(self):
        self.assertEqual(make().match("/users/me"), ("me", {}))
rootCause: Three independent bugs. The parameter pattern is .+, which matches slashes, so a parameter can swallow several segments; it must stop at the next slash. Paths are not normalised, so a trailing slash never matches. Routes are tried in registration order, so a parameter route shadows a fixed route added after it.

wrongFixes.whyWrong: Stripping every trailing slash turns the root path '/' into the empty string, so the home route no longer matches.

turns.text: Routing is wrong in three ways. Can you fix it?
Parameters should stop at a slash ([^/]+), I'll strip a trailing slash but keep '/' itself, and try fixed routes before parameter routes. Running both suites after.

test_failing: OK (3 tests)
test_regression: OK (3 tests)
Both pass. The root route still works because I only strip when the path is longer than one character.

transcript.verdict: A sound fix with the edge case handled on purpose: the root path is kept, and both suites were run.

grading.question: Why must a path parameter stop at '/'?
grading.ideal: Otherwise it matches across segments, so /users/1/posts also matches /users/<id>.

grading.question: What breaks if you rstrip('/') without a length check?
grading.ideal: The root path '/' becomes empty and no longer matches the home route.

title: Every webhook goes to the last customer
concept: Closures capture variables, not values
symptom: Acme says it stopped receiving order webhooks this morning, and Globex is asking why it gets Acme's orders. Both were registered in the same batch; Globex was the last customer in it.
failingTest:
import unittest

from hooks import Dispatcher


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_each_customer_gets_its_own_events(self):
        sent = []
        d = Dispatcher(lambda url, event: sent.append((url, event)))
        d.register([("acme", "https://acme.test/hook"), ("globex", "https://globex.test/hook")])
        d.dispatch("acme", {"order": 1})

regressionTests:
import unittest

from hooks import Dispatcher


class Regression(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.sent = []
        self.d = Dispatcher(lambda url, event: self.sent.append((url, event)))

    def test_customers_who_sign_up_later_are_added(self):
        self.d.register([("acme", "https://acme.test/hook")])
        self.d.register([("initech", "https://initech.test/hook")])
        self.d.dispatch("acme", {"order": 1})
        self.d.dispatch("initech", {"order": 2})
        self.assertEqual(
            self.sent,
            [("https://acme.test/hook", {"order": 1}), ("https://initech.test/hook", {"order": 2})],
        )

    def test_the_last_customer_in_a_batch_still_works(self):
        self.d.register([("acme", "https://acme.test/hook"), ("globex", "https://globex.test/hook")])
        self.d.dispatch("globex", {"order": 3})
        self.assertEqual(self.sent, [("https://globex.test/hook", {"order": 3})])
rootCause: Each lambda refers to the loop variable url, and a closure reads its variables when it is called, not when it is created. By the time any webhook fires, the loop has finished and url holds the last customer's address, so every handler sends there.

wrongFixes.whyWrong: partial binds the url correctly, but the rewrite replaces the whole handlers dict on every call. register runs again for each new signup, so registering Initech silently drops Acme.

turns.text: All webhooks are going to the last registered customer. Please fix it.
Classic late binding: the lambdas share the loop variable url. I replaced the loop with a dict comprehension using functools.partial, which binds each url when the handler is made. It is shorter too.
test_failing: OK (1 test)
Each customer now gets its own events.

transcript.verdict: The diagnosis is exactly right, and the tidy-up broke something else: the comprehension assigns a new dict, so each register() call wipes the customers registered before it. The docstring says register is called again on every signup. Bind the url, but keep adding to the existing dict.

grading.question: When does a Python closure read the variables it uses?
grading.ideal: When it runs. A lambda made in a loop sees the loop variable's final value unless it is bound at creation.

grading.question: Name two ways to bind the value at creation time.
grading.ideal: A default argument (url=url) or functools.partial, or a small factory function that returns the closure.
